extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public interested in manners, theatre, and moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and exempla about representing beauty, vanity, and social performance in prose and social practice; includes prescriptive maxims about what makes a person (especially a woman) truly beautiful and descriptions of performative conventions in clubs and theatre proposals. Useful for characterization and satirical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem-in-praise as admission to amorous society
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mistress, and a Poem in her Praise, will introduce any Candidate: Without the latter no one can be admitted; for he that is not in love enough to rhime, is unqualified for our Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: the Amorous Club admits members on demonstrable performance of amorous feeling — a poem in praise of a mistress — and organizes itself around secrecy, celebration of passion, and parody of formal university practices. Additional rules: 'To speak disrespectfully of any Woman, is Expulsion from our gentle Society.' Presidentship is bestowed according to 'Dignity of Passion.' Use this as a rule for fictional clubs/ceremonies: require a performative token (poem, song, toast) as a membership test and enforce behavioral prohibitions (e.g., no disrespect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty to speak in the thread of one's thoughts (club discourse style)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Man comes into the Club, he is not obliged to make any Introduction to his Discourse, but at once, as he is seating himself in his Chair, speaks in the Thread of his own Thoughts ... in this Assembly they do not meet to talk to each other, but every Man claims the full Liberty of talking to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a model of conversational style in characterization: characters may monologue, ignore direct exchange, and treat gatherings as parallel soliloquies. Props/tokens (ribbon, broken fan, old girdle) are used to sustain the private meditation. The social norm discourages direct answers and values affective display over exchange of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathetic expression and gesture as social currency
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very ordinary in the Assembly for one of a sudden to rise and make a Discourse concerning his Passion in general, and describe the Temper of his Mind in such a Manner, as that the whole Company shall join in the Description, and feel the Force of it. In this Case, if any Man has declared the Violence of his Flame in more pathetick Terms, he is made President for that Night, out of respect to his superior Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for dramatic or social scenes: rhetorical force and pathos win honor and authority. In scenes of lovers' clubs or theatrical satire, rank can be assigned by ostentatious feeling; group response validates individual display. Use rising, speeches, shared description, and physical gestures (dumb-show) to stage communal sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary maxims concerning beauty (four maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary Maxims: (1) That no Woman can be Handsome by the Force of Features alone, any more than she can be Witty only by the Help of Speech. (2) That Pride destroys all Symmetry and Grace, and Affectation is a more terrible Enemy to fine Faces than the Small-Pox. (3) That no Woman is capable of being Beautiful, who is not incapable of being False. (4) That what would be Odious in a Friend, is Deformity in a Mistress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms form a prescriptive rubric for portraying female characters and the meaning of beauty in fiction: beauty is not merely anatomical but moral and behavioral; pride and affectation undermine aesthetic appeal; truthfulness (or the implication about falsehood in the original phrasing) and social suitability are central. Use these maxims to guide characterization, contrast superficial ornament with inner virtues, and dramatize consequences of vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art of assisting beauty = embellish by virtuous qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The true Art of assisting Beauty consists in Embellishing the whole Person by the proper Ornaments of virtuous and commendable Qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for writers and moralists: when 'improving' or describing beauty, emphasize virtues (good humour, innocence, piety, truth) that animate appearance. Examples offered: Milton's Adam describing Eve by 'lustre of her Mind' and Ben Jonson's epitaph. Use internal qualities in narration to make outward beauty credible and affecting; cosmetics alone entertain the eye but do not touch the heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cosmetic quacks; promote genuine methods
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be an acceptable Service to take them out of the Hands of Quacks and Pretenders, and to prevent their imposing upon themselves, by discovering to them the true Secret and Art of improving Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about beauty cultures or beauty industries, criticize charlatanism and foreground reliable, moral means (education, accomplishments, virtues). For social satire, contrast learned physicians or quacks who profit from false remedies; show consequences of reliance on false helps and the social economy around cosmetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability and feasibility of theatrical spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Some at the Table urged that a Puppet-Show was not a suitable Entertainment for Alexander the Great; and that it might be introduced more properly, if we suppose the Conqueror touched upon that part of India which is said to be inhabited by the Pigmies. ... the Bull-baiting only excepted, which cannot possibly be exhibited in the Theatre, by Reason of the Lowness of the Roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a rubric for designing plays/entertainments: ensure that spectacle matches subject-matter and setting, and respect practical staging constraints (stage height, weapons, animals). Satirical mash-ups (anachronistic amusements) may be comic but risk incoherence; practitioners should assess fit and technical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess originality and feasibility of projects (satire of projectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Projector ... said that the Thought ... was not originally his own, but that he had taken the Hint of it from several Performances which he had seen upon our Stage ... that after the Reconciliation of these two Kings they might invite one another to Dinner, and either of them entertain his Guest with the German Artist, Mr. Pinkethman's Heathen Gods, or any of the like Diversions, which shall then chance to be in vogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric for evaluating proposals: check for originality, avoid cobbling disparate popular bits into a single 'scheme' without coherence; verify available resources and logistics rather than blindly accepting grandiose claims. The satire highlights common projector fallacies: borrowing uncredited ideas, jamming current entertainments into unrelated narratives, and promising convenient supply chains (e.g., musicians from Smyrna) without plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional license for wits to use masks/pseudonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: That Wits were privileged to wear what Masks they pleased in all Ages; and that a Vizard had been the constant Crown of their Labours, which was generally presented them by the Hand of some Satyr, and sometimes of Apollo himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for authorship and persona in satire: using a mask, pseudonym, or satirical persona is an established literary practice and may be defended by appeal to tradition (frontispiece imagery, examples from Juvenal). For creative-writing, consider adopting a persona to enable sharper satire or to protect authorial identity; such masks are rhetorically meaningful and historically grounded.
